messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Tutor
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 55

The patient is a 35-year-old African woman who works as a private tutor. She came to therapy after her partner encouraged her, though she was hesitant, describing herself as “fine” before the first session. Over several weeks, she has begun to share her story.

The trauma happened four years ago, when she was tutoring at a small community center. A colleague she trusted asked her to stay late to help organize materials. She agreed. After the other staff left, he locked the door. She describes the assault in fragments: the pressure of his hand over her mouth, the sound of her own breathing, the feeling of the cold floor against her back. She did not scream. She did not fight. She tells me, “I just went somewhere else.” She never reported it. She quit the center the next week and told no one, not even her family.

In the months that followed, she moved to a different part of the city and found work as a private tutor. She began seeing a man she met through a mutual friend. He is kind, patient, and knows nothing about the assault. She has not told him. She says she is afraid he will see her as “broken.” Their relationship is warm, but she avoids being alone with him at night. When he reaches for her in bed, her body goes rigid. She pretends to be tired, or she turns away. She feels guilty, but she cannot explain why she reacts this way.

Her work as a tutor has become her refuge. She spends long hours preparing lessons, often staying at the library until it closes. She focuses intensely on her students, especially the younger ones, and she is careful never to be alone in a room with a male student. The door is always open. She scans the hallway before entering any empty classroom. She no longer takes evening appointments. If a male student is running late, she reschedules. She tells herself it is professionalism, but she knows it is fear.

At home, she avoids the news. Violence against women, court cases, even fictional scenes in movies — these trigger a tightness in her chest and a need to leave the room. She has nightmares about being chased, about a heavy weight pressing her down. She wakes up sweating, her heart racing. On those nights, she lies still and watches the shadows until dawn. She does not wake her partner.

She has difficulty trusting her own memory. She often replays the assault, asking herself if she could have done something different. She feels dirty, as if something about her invited it. She has not returned to that part of the city. She avoids public transportation at certain times. She carries her keys between her fingers when she walks to her car.

Her partner has noticed her distance. He asks if she is unhappy, if he has done something wrong. She reassures him, but the words feel hollow. She wants to be close to him, but the fear is louder than the wanting. She feels trapped between her past and her present, unable to speak the truth, unable to move past it. She tells me that some days she feels like she is still on that cold floor.
